section.title: Philip in Samaria and the Ethiopian Eunuch
section.sectionRationale: The stoning of Stephen unleashes a persecution that scatters the Jerusalem church, and the very violence meant to crush the gospel becomes the wind that carries it outward. Philip, one of the seven, preaches Christ in Samaria, the old rival of the Jews, and the despised Samaritans believe. Then an angel and the Spirit send Philip to a desert road to meet an African court official reading Isaiah, and the gospel reaches to the ends of the earth in a single chariot.
section.thesis: The scattering of the church cannot stop the word but spreads it, so that in one chapter the gospel crosses the ancient wall between Jew and Samaritan and reaches an African official at the edge of the known world, proving that the risen Christ is gathering a people from every nation.
section.frameNote: Four movements: persecution scatters the church out of Jerusalem; Philip proclaims Christ in Samaria and Simon the sorcerer is exposed; the apostles come and the Samaritans receive the Spirit; and Philip meets the Ethiopian eunuch, opens Isaiah to him, and baptizes him.

units.label: Persecution scatters the church
units.note: the gospel driven out of Jerusalem

verses.text: And Saul was there, giving approval to Stephen’s death. On that day a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered throughout Judea and Samaria.
God-fearing men buried Stephen and mourned deeply over him.
But Saul began to destroy the church. Going from house to house, he dragged off men and women and put them in prison.

units.label: Philip proclaims Christ in Samaria
units.note: Samaria receives the word, and even Simon believes

verses.text: Those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went.
Philip went down to a city in Samaria and proclaimed the Christ to them.
The crowds all paid close attention to Philip’s message and to the signs they saw him perform.
With loud shrieks, unclean spirits came out of many who were possessed, and many of the paralyzed and lame were healed.
So there was great joy in that city.
Prior to that time, a man named Simon had practiced sorcery in the city and astounded the people of Samaria. He claimed to be someone great,
and all the people, from the least to the greatest, heeded his words and said, “This man is the divine power called the Great Power.”
They paid close attention to him because he had astounded them for a long time with his sorcery.
But when they believed Philip as he preached the gospel of the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women.
Even Simon himself believed and was baptized. He followed Philip closely and was astounded by the great signs and miracles he observed.

units.label: The apostles come and the Spirit is given
units.note: the Samaritans receive the Spirit, and Simon is rebuked

verses.text: When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them.
On their arrival, they prayed for them to receive the Holy Spirit.
For the Holy Spirit had not yet fallen upon any of them; they had simply been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.
Then Peter and John laid their hands on them, and they received the {{pneuma|Holy Spirit}}.
When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money.
“Give me this power as well,” he said, “so that everyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.”
But Peter replied, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could buy the gift of God with money!
You have no part or share in our ministry, because your heart is not right before God.
Repent, therefore, of your wickedness, and pray to the Lord. Perhaps He will forgive you for the intent of your heart.
For I see that you are poisoned by bitterness and captive to iniquity.”
Then Simon answered, “Pray to the Lord for me, so that nothing you have said may happen to me.”
And after Peter and John had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel in many of the Samaritan villages.

units.label: Philip and the Ethiopian eunuch
units.note: the gospel reaches an African official at the ends of the earth

verses.text: Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Get up and go south to the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.”
So he started out, and on his way he met an Ethiopian {{eunouchos|eunuch}}, a court official in charge of the entire treasury of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians. He had gone to Jerusalem to worship,
and on his return was sitting in his chariot reading Isaiah the prophet.
The Spirit said to Philip, “Go over to that chariot and stay by it.”
So Philip ran up and heard the man reading Isaiah the prophet. “Do you understand what you are reading?” Philip asked.
“How can I,” he said, “unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.
The eunuch was reading this passage of Scripture: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before the shearer is silent, so He did not open His mouth.
In His humiliation He was deprived of justice. Who can recount His descendants? For His life was removed from the earth.”
“Tell me,” said the eunuch, “who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?”
Then Philip began with this very Scripture and told him the {{euangelizo|good news}} about Jesus.
As they traveled along the road and came to some water, the eunuch said, “Look, here is water! What is there to prevent me from being baptized?”
And he gave orders to stop the chariot. Then both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water, and Philip {{baptizo|baptized}} him.
When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, but went on his way rejoicing.
But Philip appeared at Azotus and traveled through that region, preaching the gospel in all the towns until he came to Caesarea.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. Here it is the Holy Spirit, promised by the risen Christ and poured out at Pentecost. In Samaria the same Spirit who fell on the Jerusalem believers is given to the Samaritans, publicly binding them into the one people of God.

eunouchos.gloss: A eunuch, often a trusted official in a royal court. As a foreigner and a physically marked man, he stood on the margins of the temple, yet Isaiah 56 had promised eunuchs and foreigners a name and a place among God's people, a promise the gospel now fulfils in him.

euangelizo.gloss: To announce good news, to preach the gospel. Philip opens Isaiah 53 and preaches the good news about Jesus, showing that the suffering servant led like a lamb to the slaughter is the Christ crucified and risen for sinners.

baptizo.gloss: To immerse, to baptize. The eunuch's request, what is there to prevent me, and his immersion in the water mark him openly as a disciple of Jesus, received into the church without regard to his nation or his status.

basic.context: Stephen has just been killed, and a fierce persecution scatters the Jerusalem believers, though the apostles stay. What looks like disaster becomes the engine of mission: the scattered believers preach wherever they go. Philip goes to Samaria, a people the Jews despised, and they believe. Then God sends him to a desert road to meet an Ethiopian official, and the gospel reaches an African at the edge of the map. The key questions are: why must the church be scattered, why do the Samaritans receive the Spirit only when the apostles come, and what does it mean that this foreign eunuch is welcomed in?
basic.hermeneutics: Read this chapter as the map of Acts 1:8 unfolding: from Jerusalem, into Judea and Samaria, and toward the ends of the earth. The Samaritan episode is a hinge, so the delay of the Spirit until Peter and John arrive is best read as God visibly uniting a once-divided people to the apostolic church, not as a rule that conversion and the Spirit normally come apart. The eunuch story shows how personal, Scripture-centred evangelism works.
basic.originalLanguages: The Samaritans receive the pneuma, the Holy Spirit, the same gift given at Pentecost. Philip meets an eunouchos, a court official and outsider, and tells him the good news, euangelizo, from Isaiah. The man asks to be baptized, baptizo, and is received openly as a disciple. The words trace the movement of the one gospel across old boundaries.
basic.typology: The Isaiah passage the eunuch reads, the lamb led to the slaughter who does not open His mouth, is fulfilled in Jesus, the suffering servant. The eunuch himself fulfils Isaiah 56, where God promises the foreigner and the eunuch a place and a name among His people. Philip's snatching away recalls the prophets carried by the Spirit.
basic.christ: Philip preaches Christ in Samaria and Christ from Isaiah 53 to the eunuch. The whole chapter is about proclaiming the name of Jesus. The servant who was humbled and deprived of justice, whose life was removed from the earth, is the crucified and risen Lord, and the good news about Him is what turns strangers into worshippers who go on their way rejoicing.
basic.god: God is sovereign over the scattering and the mission. He directs Philip by an angel and by the Spirit, arranges the meeting on the desert road, and gives His Spirit to the Samaritans. He shows no partiality, opening His people to Samaritan and African alike, and He exposes and warns Simon, whose heart is not right.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 1:8 sets the plan the chapter follows. Isaiah 53:7-8 is the very text the eunuch reads. Isaiah 56:3-8 promises the foreigner and eunuch a place. John 4 shows Jesus Himself reaching Samaria first.
basic.oneStory: This is the gospel breaking out of Jerusalem. The wall between Jew and Samaritan falls, and an African official carries the news home, a living picture of the promise that in Abraham's seed all nations would be blessed. The scattering that seemed to end the church actually launched it toward the ends of the earth.

context.literary:
Acts 8 is a chapter of two journeys, and Luke builds it as a pair. The first is a mission to a crowd: Philip goes down to a city, the whole city pays attention, there is great joy, and the apostles come from Jerusalem to confirm it. The second is a mission to one man: Philip is told to go to a road, there is no crowd and no city, and the apostles are nowhere. Luke deliberately sets side by side the mass response and the single conversion, so that the reader sees that the same gospel works at both scales.

The chapter is also stitched together by small repetitions. The adjective 'great' runs through it like a drumbeat: a great persecution, 8:1; great joy, 8:8; Simon who claimed to be someone great and was called the Great Power, 8:9-10; and Simon amazed at the great signs, 8:13. The point is gentle but sharp. The only 'great' that the chapter finally honours is the joy that comes from the word, and the 'great' man is the one who ends up asking for prayer, 8:24. The verb for astonishment tells the same story: Simon astounded the crowds, 8:9 and 8:11, and now he is himself astounded, 8:13.

Joy brackets the two halves. The city has 'great joy,' 8:8, and the eunuch 'went on his way rejoicing,' 8:39. Between them lies the one dark scene, Simon, who is the only person in the chapter whose heart is described as 'not right,' 8:21. Luke leaves him unresolved. His last words are a request for prayer, and the narrative moves on before we learn what he did with it.

The movements follow Acts 1:8. Verse 1 scatters the church into Judea and Samaria; the eunuch's road runs south toward Africa and the ends of the earth. Notice also that the two halves of the chapter are driven by God from outside the apostles: persecution does the first and an angel and the Spirit the second.
context.historical:
Samaria was the old capital of the northern kingdom. When Assyria conquered it, the king settled foreign peoples in its towns, 2 Kings 17:24, and the mixed community that resulted worshipped the LORD while keeping its own temple tradition on Mount Gerizim. By the first century the quarrel was bitter. John explains that Jews did not associate with Samaritans, John 4:9, and the woman at the well raises the dispute about the mountain, John 4:20. James and John once wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village that refused Jesus, Luke 9:52-54. When Philip, a Hellenist chosen in Acts 6, preaches Christ there, he is crossing the sharpest ethnic boundary in his own world, and it fits that a Greek-speaking Jew does so first.

Luke's note that all but the apostles were scattered in 8:1 leaves open why the apostles stayed. The text does not say. One possible reason is leadership and witness: they were the ones who had been with Jesus and who were publicly known to the people of the city, and the church there continued to meet.

The Ethiopian is a man from Cush, the land south of Egypt along the Nile. 'Candace' is not a personal name but the title of the queen mother of that kingdom, as the BSB footnote notes, and the official was in charge of her treasury. He is a man of high standing and money, yet as a eunuch he would have been excluded from full membership of the assembly under the Law, Deuteronomy 23:1. He has travelled hundreds of miles to worship in Jerusalem and owns a scroll of Isaiah, an expensive possession in that age, and reads it aloud, as readers then usually did, which is how Philip hears him.

The road from Jerusalem to Gaza ran into the south-west. Luke's phrase in 8:26 can mean either 'go south' or 'go at midday', and the closing remark that 'this is desert' could refer to the road or to the town. None of the options changes the story. Philip then turns up at Azotus, the old Philistine town of Ashdod, and works his way north along the coast to Caesarea, 8:40, where we meet him again years later, Acts 21:8.
context.canonical:
The two halves of this chapter fulfil two lines of Old Testament promise that Israel had long held apart from each other. The first is the reunion of the divided people. Ezekiel 37:15-22 sees two sticks, Judah and Joseph, made one in God's hand, and Samaria was the heart of the old northern kingdom. When the Samaritans receive the word, the two Israels are for the first time gathered under one Lord, and Peter and John are sent from Jerusalem to be certain that the new believers are not a separate and rival body.

The second line is the pilgrimage of the nations. Psalm 68:31 says that Cush will stretch out her hands to God, Psalm 87:4 lists Cush among those born in Zion, and Zephaniah 3:10 pictures worshippers coming 'from beyond the rivers of Cush.' Isaiah 56:3-8 goes further and names the very man who stands on that road: the foreigner and the eunuch, told not to say that they are excluded. The Lord promises the eunuch 'a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters,' 56:5. The man in the chariot is not the first Cushite to be welcomed; Ebed-melech, a Cushite court official, is promised rescue because he trusted in the Lord, Jeremiah 38:7 and 39:18.

The passage the eunuch reads is Isaiah 53:7-8, the fourth Servant Song, and Luke gives the wording of the Greek Old Testament. This is the passage that Peter and Paul and the writers of the New Testament repeatedly apply to Jesus, and here it is applied by an evangelist to an official who has no preconceptions. The chapter ends with the beginning of Philip's travels, which leads on to Cornelius at Caesarea, the next frontier crossed, Acts 10.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants his readers to see that the scattering of the church is not an accident of persecution but the way the risen Lord is carrying out the plan He announced in Acts 1:8. The enemy meant to extinguish the church, and the Lord used the fire to light more lamps. A church that is tempted to read hardship as a sign that God has stepped away is reminded of this chapter.

He also wants us to feel that evangelism is both big and personal. The first half is public, with miracles, crowds and apostles. The second half is a private conversation over a scroll. Luke does not choose between them. He shows that both are the Spirit's work and that the Spirit may speak by an angel one hour and by an open Bible the next.

He wants the question of the Samaritan reception answered with care. The believers were baptized, and then, for a time, the Spirit had not fallen. Luke tells it so that the apostles' hands become a visible bridge between the old people and the new, and so that no later believer in Samaria could say that Jerusalem had not recognised them. And Simon is there as a warning: it is possible to be impressed by power and not to know the Lord.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what happened; it does not hand us a method. The Spirit's delayed coming in 8:15-17 is described as something unusual, and Luke uses the explanatory note 'for the Holy Spirit had not yet fallen upon any of them,' so the delay itself needed to be explained. It is not offered as a normal pattern. Later in Acts the Spirit falls as the gospel is believed, 10:44 and 11:17, and Paul writes that everyone who belongs to Christ has the Spirit, Romans 8:9.

Philip's sudden removal in 8:39 is an event, not a command to expect to be carried across the countryside. What does carry over is the readiness: Philip gets up and goes, 8:27, runs to the chariot, 8:30, and begins with the passage the man is already reading. That is a pattern for listening, asking a question, and starting where a person is, which any believer can imitate.

Simon's request is also not a pattern but a warning. The gift of God cannot be bought, and a ministry that treats the Spirit as a possession to be traded is condemned by the first apostle who sees it. The church later called such trading simony, after Simon, and the principle stays in force wherever spiritual office or influence is for sale.

debates.question: Why did the Samaritans receive the Spirit only when Peter and John came?

views.label: A one-time, salvation-historical moment
views.case: Acts 1:8 lays out a sequence: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, the ends of the earth. Each new group in Acts, Jews at Pentecost, Samaritans here, Gentiles in Acts 10, receives the Spirit in a way the church could see. The apostles' presence here keeps the old rivalry from producing two churches, and the same pattern is not repeated afterwards. This is a widely held reading among those who hold that the Spirit comes at conversion.

views.label: Their faith was incomplete or defective
views.case: Luke says they had been baptized only 'into the name of the Lord Jesus,' 8:16, and Simon the sorcerer's belief proves shallow. On this reading the Samaritans first accepted a message about signs and needed to be taught more. The difficulty is that Luke says in 8:12 that they 'believed' and in 8:14 that they had 'received the word of God,' words he uses of true conversion.

views.label: A second experience after conversion is the normal pattern
views.case: Some traditions read 8:14-17, together with Acts 19:1-7, as evidence that believers may be converted and then receive the Spirit in a distinct later moment. Opponents point out that the case in Acts 10, where the Spirit falls as people first believe, and Paul's teaching in 1 Corinthians 12:13 that all were baptized in one Spirit, treat reception as part of becoming a Christian.

debates.bearing: Luke explains the delay as exceptional, and the unity of the new church with the old is the clearest reason. The way a reader answers affects how normal the experience of 8:17 is thought to be.

debates.question: Was Simon truly converted?

views.label: He believed genuinely and then fell into a serious sin
views.case: The verb is the same in 8:12 and 8:13, 'believed,' and he was baptized and followed Philip. Peter's rebuke is addressed to someone who can still 'repent' and 'pray to the Lord,' 8:22, and Simon's reply asks for prayer. On this reading a true believer has stumbled badly and is being called back.

views.label: He was impressed but never regenerate
views.case: Peter says his heart is 'not right before God' and that he has 'no part or share' in the ministry, and describes him as 'poisoned by bitterness and captive to iniquity,' 8:21-23. The wording echoes Deuteronomy 29:18, which warns of a root that bears poisonous and bitter fruit in the heart of one who turns from the Lord. John 2:23-25 shows that belief prompted by signs is not always saving, and Simon is held by the signs, 8:13.

views.label: Luke leaves it open on purpose
views.case: Peter's 'Perhaps He will forgive you,' 8:22, and Luke's silence about what happened next suggest that the story is a warning to the reader rather than a verdict on Simon. The point is the condition of the heart, and each reader is invited to put the question to himself.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is taken, the application is the same: being near signs, ministry and the church is not the same as having a heart that is right before God, and the way back is repentance and prayer.

debates.question: Is Acts 8:37 part of the text?

views.label: It is a later addition
views.case: The BSB omits the verse and notes that the Textus Receptus includes it: 'If you believe with all your heart, you may be baptized,' with the eunuch's reply that he believes that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. The verse is absent from the earliest and best Greek manuscripts and appears to have been added by copyists who wanted the baptismal confession spelled out.

views.label: It reflects genuine early practice though not Luke's original
views.case: Even if it is not original, the verse shows that early Christians read the story as a confession of faith before baptism. The thing that is certain from the earlier verses is the question that all Christians were asking: what hinders me from being baptized, 8:36.

debates.bearing: The story does not depend on the verse. The eunuch asks to be baptized because he has heard the good news about Jesus, 8:35, and his joy afterwards is Luke's own evidence of faith.

study.originalLanguages:
The scattering of 8:1 and 8:4 uses diaspeiro, to disperse as seed is scattered. The noun diaspora comes from the same root. The persecution does not merely drive the believers out; in Luke's wording they are sown, and the word goes with them. When they go, they 'preach the word,' 8:4, using the verb euangelizomai, a single word for gospel preaching that Luke repeats in 8:12, 8:25 and 8:40 as Philip's habit.

Simon is described by the verb mageuo, to practise sorcery, and the people say he is the Great Power. Luke then uses the verb existemi, to astonish, for what Simon did to the people in 8:9 and 8:11, and he uses the same verb for what happened to Simon in 8:13 when he saw Philip's signs. The sorcerer who amazed the crowds is himself amazed. The word is a favourite of Luke for the response to the supernatural, and its repetition here puts Simon among the astonished rather than the believing.

Peter's word for the Spirit in 8:20 is dorea, a free gift. The same word describes the Spirit in Acts 2:38, 10:45 and 11:17. To think it could be bought, ktasthai, to acquire, shows that Simon had not grasped what a gift is. The verb for the Spirit's coming in 8:16, epipipto, to fall upon, matches the language used of Cornelius's household, 10:44 and 11:15, and that is what ties the Samaritan episode to the opening of the door to the Gentiles.

In the desert road scene Luke uses a pair of verbs that play on one another. Philip asks, 'Do you understand what you are reading?' using ginosko and anaginosko, to know and to read, as though to say, 'Do you know what you are reading?', 8:30. The eunuch replies that he needs someone to guide him, hodegeo, a verb built on hodos, the road, and the one on whom the answer depends is also the Spirit who in John 16:13 hodegesei, will guide you into all truth.

The description of the lamb in Isaiah 53 comes in the Greek wording, and 'Who can recount His descendants?' uses genea, which means both descendants and generation. Then Luke writes that Philip 'opened his mouth,' anoixas to stoma, 8:35, where the Servant 'does not open His mouth,' 8:32. The silent Lamb is made to speak through a man who opens his mouth to tell about Him.

Finally, the eunuch's question, 'What is there to prevent me from being baptized?' uses the verb koluo, to hinder, which returns in Peter's question, 'Can anyone withhold the water,' 10:47, and in 11:17, 'who was I to hinder the work of God?' The same word runs through the story of the Gentile door from beginning to end. And after the baptism the Spirit 'carried Philip away,' using harpazo, to snatch, and Philip 'appeared at Azotus,' literally was found there, 8:39-40.

typology.type: The Lamb led to the slaughter, Isaiah 53 and Acts 8:32
typology.fulfillment: The eunuch reads of a sheep led to slaughter and a lamb silent before the shearer. Philip begins from that Scripture and tells him the good news about Jesus, 8:35. The correspondence is Christ's death: He is silent before His accusers, Matthew 27:12-14, and He is called 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' John 1:29, and the lamb without blemish whose blood redeems, 1 Peter 1:19. The escalation is that Isaiah's Servant dies for the many and is vindicated, and the Passover and sacrificial lambs now find their meaning in One Lamb. The type falls short in that no animal could take sin away; the Lamb of God is also the Shepherd and the Priest.

typology.type: The eunuch and the foreigner welcomed, Isaiah 56:3-5
typology.fulfillment: The Law excluded a man with crushed or severed genitals from the assembly, Deuteronomy 23:1, but Isaiah 56:3-5 promises that the eunuch who holds fast to the covenant will have a name better than sons and daughters. The Ethiopian official, returning from worship and reading the same prophet, is the first named person to step into that promise, and he is baptized into the church without any condition beyond faith. The escalation is that in Christ there is a people not defined by birth, Galatians 3:28. The type falls short only in that Isaiah foresaw a house of prayer for all peoples, Isaiah 56:7, and the eunuch is its first guest, not its last.

typology.type: The divided kingdom made one, Ezekiel 37:15-22
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel took two sticks, Judah and Joseph, and joined them in his hand as a sign that God would make the divided people one. The Samaritans were the heirs of the northern kingdom, and the apostles from Jerusalem lay hands on them so that the two halves are one church. In Christ the escalation goes beyond reuniting Israel: He is Himself the one Shepherd of one flock, John 10:16, who makes Jew and Gentile one in His body, Ephesians 2:14-16. The type falls short because Ezekiel's promise stayed within the people of Israel and left its larger scope for later revelation.

typology.type: The prophet carried by the Spirit, 1 Kings 18:12 and Acts 8:39
typology.fulfillment: When Obadiah feared that the Spirit of the LORD would carry Elijah off, 1 Kings 18:12, and the sons of the prophets feared the Spirit had set Elijah down on a mountain, 2 Kings 2:16, they described a servant moved at the Spirit's will. Ezekiel was lifted up by the Spirit in the same way, Ezekiel 3:12. Philip's sudden removal in 8:39 is the same pattern in the new age, and the Spirit of the Lord is now the Spirit of Christ poured out on all flesh. The correspondence points to the Spirit's freedom, but the type has no great fulfilment of its own; it simply shows that the work of Elijah and Ezekiel continues in the church.

study.christ:
The chapter's two halves each show Christ proclaimed in a different way. In Samaria Philip 'proclaimed the Christ,' 8:5, and later the message is described as 'the gospel of the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ,' 8:12. The Samaritans have been waiting for a Messiah; the woman at the well told her town that a man had told her everything she had done, John 4:29, and Jesus Himself stayed in Samaria two days before He ever sent anyone there. Philip is walking into a field in which Jesus had already sown, John 4:35-38.

On the desert road Christ is found in Isaiah 53. The eunuch's question, 'Who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?', is the question Jesus' own followers had to ask, and Luke's Gospel shows the answer at the end: the risen Lord on another road explained 'what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself,' Luke 24:27. Philip does the same and begins from this very text. Every phrase in the passage the eunuch reads finds its counterpart in the passion. He is led as a lamb, Acts 8:32; deprived of justice in a trial that ended in a verdict that cannot be defended, Luke 23:4 and John 19:6; and his life is removed from the earth in a death that is also a lifting up, John 12:32. The text goes on past where the eunuch stops, to the Servant who sees the light of life and justifies many, Isaiah 53:11.

The risen Christ is also behind the chapter's movement. The Spirit's gift to the Samaritans, the angel's word to Philip, and the Spirit's instruction at the chariot are all the work of the One who said He would send the Spirit, John 16:7, and who told His disciples they would be witnesses in Samaria, Acts 1:8. The name by which they are baptized is 'the name of the Lord Jesus,' 8:16.

A caution is useful. Luke gives us only a single line of Philip's sermon, that he told the eunuch 'the good news about Jesus,' and we should not invent what else he said. The text itself shows what mattered: Philip began where the man was and brought him to Jesus. That is the pattern the church has to follow.
study.god:
The God of this chapter acts from outside the apostles' plans. He lets persecution break out and uses it for mission; He sends an angel to Philip and the Spirit to the chariot; He moves Philip from a revival in Samaria to a single man in a wilderness. Luke wants us to see that the church does not set its own agenda. Philip was in the middle of a city-wide movement and was told to leave it for one traveller. That is the freedom of the God who numbers the sparrows.

He is also the God who removes the ancient barriers. The Samaritans were set aside as a mixed and heretical people, and the eunuch's body had put him outside the assembly. Neither is excluded. The same God who made Israel a distinct people now makes them part of a larger family, and He does it by a gift, the Spirit, that cannot be earned or bought. The phrase Peter will use in Acts 10:34, that God shows no favouritism, is already being acted out.

He is holy. Simon's offer meets an instant and severe rebuke, 'May your silver perish with you,' 8:20, because the gift of God is not a commodity. The same Lord who gives freely also searches the heart, and Peter sees what is in Simon's: bitterness and bondage, 8:23. The God of grace is not indifferent to the state of the heart.

He is merciful to the one who has failed. Peter does not say that Simon is beyond hope; he says, 'Repent, therefore, of your wickedness, and pray to the Lord. Perhaps He will forgive you,' 8:22. The gospel's invitation stands even at the point of a rebuke.

He is the God who speaks through His word. The Spirit does not give the eunuch a vision; He sends a man to open a scroll that was already in the eunuch's hands. The sovereign God uses the means He has already given, the written word and a person willing to explain it. For worship, the chapter teaches us to hold together a wide welcome and a clear call: the doors are open to every nation, and they open onto a gift that is received by faith and not purchased by power.

crossReferences.note: The risen Lord promised witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. Acts 8:1 scatters believers into Judea and Samaria and the eunuch carries the word south toward the edge of the known world. The chapter is the programme in motion.

Jesus had already spent two days in a Samaritan town and many believed. Philip's reception in Samaria reaps what Jesus began, and Jesus' words about fields white for harvest, John 4:35-38, are borne out.

James and John once wanted fire from heaven on a Samaritan village that refused Jesus. In Acts 8:15 John comes to the same land to pray that the Samaritans may receive the Holy Spirit. The disciple who wanted judgment on Samaria is the one who brings the Spirit to it.

The eunuch is reading the silent Lamb, humiliated and deprived of justice. Acts 8:33 follows the wording of the Greek Old Testament, and Philip takes it as a prophecy of Jesus. The Servant's suffering is the centre of the good news.

The eunuch is promised a memorial and a name better than sons and daughters, and the foreigner is told not to say that he is excluded. The man in the chariot is the first named person to walk into this promise, which is why the story makes so much of his body and his office.

The psalm says that Cush will stretch out her hands to God. The Ethiopian official who has come to Jerusalem to worship and who receives the gospel is a first fruit of this prophecy, and it explains why Luke bothers to name his country.
The prophet pictures worshippers from beyond the rivers of Cush bringing offerings to the Lord. The Ethiopian already on his way home from worship in Jerusalem is a sign of that gathering.

The Law barred a man with crushed or severed genitals from the assembly of the LORD. The eunuch's outsider status is real, and it is the Law's own word that Isaiah 56 reverses. The baptism in Acts 8:38 shows how fully Christ has opened the assembly.

Moses warns that no root among the people should bear poisonous and bitter fruit. Peter's description of Simon as poisoned by bitterness, Acts 8:23, draws on that language. The man's heart is a root of the very thing the covenant warned against.

The Spirit falls on Cornelius's household as Peter speaks, and Peter asks, 'Can anyone withhold the water to baptize these people?' It is the same question the eunuch asked in 8:36, with the same verb, and it shows that the road from Samaria and the desert leads straight to the Gentile door.

Obadiah feared that the Spirit of the LORD would carry Elijah off to an unknown place. Philip's removal in Acts 8:39 is the same kind of event and places him among the prophets who were moved by the Spirit.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with one family and one command to fill the earth, and by Genesis 11 the nations are scattered at Babel and divided by language. The promise to Abraham begins to reverse this: in his seed all the families of the earth will be blessed, Genesis 12:3. For most of the Old Testament the answer seems small, a single nation with a few visitors and a few believing outsiders, Rahab, Ruth, Naaman, Ebed-melech, who show the promise is alive.

The prophets enlarge the promise. Isaiah sees the foreigner and the eunuch welcomed to God's house, Isaiah 56:3-8, and the Servant who suffers, Isaiah 53, is also the one who is given as a light to the nations, Isaiah 49:6. Acts 8 is where those two lines meet on a road: the man from the edge of the world is reading the suffering Servant and asks to be baptized into His people.

The scattering of 8:1 also echoes Babel, though it works in the opposite direction. At Babel the people were scattered in judgment; here the people of God are scattered in persecution and carry a message with them. By the end of the chapter Philip is travelling along the coast towards Caesarea, preaching in every town, and the way is prepared for the next crossing of a boundary in Acts 10. Pentecost reversed Babel's confusion of languages; Acts 8 begins to reverse its division of peoples.

The story comes to rest in the vision of Revelation, where people from every tribe, language, people and nation stand before the throne, Revelation 7:9. The eunuch's journey is an early step toward that crowd, and the Samaritans, who were once the most hated neighbours of Israel, stand beside the Jews. The scattering that looked like an ending was the beginning of the gathering, and the joy of the road in 8:39 is a foretaste of the joy of that great multitude.

sermon.title: Personal Evangelism (Acts 8:26-40)
sermon.why: Begg walks through Philip's desert encounter with the Ethiopian eunuch, showing God as the director of evangelism who arranges the meeting, prepares the seeker, and saves through the plain preaching of Christ from Isaiah, exactly the climax of this study.

quiz.q: What did the persecution after Stephen's death actually accomplish?

options.text: It scattered the believers, who preached the word wherever they went, spreading the gospel outward.
options.note: Luke shows the scattering carrying the gospel into Judea and Samaria, fulfilling Acts 1:8.

options.text: It drove the apostles out of Jerusalem to begin the mission.
options.note: The mission did advance, but the text says all except the apostles were scattered; the apostles stayed in Jerusalem.

options.text: It silenced the church for a season until things calmed down.
options.note: The opposite happened; far from being silenced, the scattered believers preached everywhere.

options.text: It ended the growth of the church in that region.
options.note: The church grew and spread; the persecution served the gospel rather than stopping it.

quiz.q: Why is it significant that Philip preached to the Samaritans?

options.text: It crossed a deep, old hostility between Jews and Samaritans, showing the gospel gathers a once-divided people into one church.
options.note: The Samaritan mission is a hinge, healing an ancient division under the apostles.

options.text: It reached a nearby region so the gospel could spread more efficiently.
options.note: True geographically, but it understates the theological weight of crossing the Jew and Samaritan divide.

options.text: It proved the Samaritans had always secretly believed the same faith.
options.note: The point is not hidden agreement but that former rivals were now brought together in Christ.

options.text: It showed the gospel was only ever meant for the descendants of Israel.
options.note: The chapter shows the reverse, the gospel reaching beyond Israel to Samaritan and African alike.

quiz.q: How is the delay of the Spirit until Peter and John arrive best understood?

options.text: As a unique, transitional moment where God visibly bound the Samaritans into the one apostolic church.
options.note: This reading fits the hinge setting and guards the unity of a once-divided people.

options.text: As a fixed rule that the Spirit is always received in a second stage after believing.
options.note: This over-reads one exceptional event as a universal pattern, against passages where the Spirit comes at conversion.

options.text: As a sign that the Samaritans' first faith was not yet real faith.
options.note: Luke says Samaria received the word of God; their faith was genuine, not counterfeit.

options.text: As God honouring the apostles' role at this particular turning point in the church's history.
options.note: True and important, but it needs the fuller point that God was uniting Samaria to the whole church, not merely honouring the apostles.

quiz.q: What was wrong with Simon's request to buy the power to give the Spirit?

options.text: He tried to purchase the gift of God with money, revealing a heart not right before God.
options.note: Peter names both the sin, buying God's gift, and its root, a wrong heart.

options.text: He wanted spiritual power for himself rather than to serve others.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but the sharpest issue is treating God's free gift as something for sale.

options.text: He had not been baptized and so had no right to ask.
options.note: Simon had in fact believed and been baptized; the problem was his heart, not a missing rite.

options.text: He was never interested in the things of God at all.
options.note: He had followed Philip and was astounded by the signs; his error was corrupt motive, not total indifference.

quiz.q: What does Philip preach to the Ethiopian eunuch from Isaiah?

options.text: The good news about Jesus, the suffering servant led like a lamb to the slaughter.
options.note: Philip begins with Isaiah 53 and tells him the good news about Jesus.

options.text: That the Scriptures are difficult and need a teacher to explain them.
options.note: The eunuch did need a guide, but Philip's actual message was Christ crucified and risen, not merely the need for interpretation.

options.text: A set of moral rules the eunuch must keep to be accepted by God.
options.note: Philip preaches the person of Jesus, not a ladder of rules; the man is received by faith and baptism.

options.text: That his foreign birth barred him from being part of God's people.
options.note: The reverse is true; the eunuch is welcomed and baptized, fulfilling Isaiah's promise to the foreigner.

questions: The believers preached wherever the scattering sent them. When life has uprooted or unsettled you, how might God be using even that to spread His word through you?
Philip went to Samaria, a people his own culture despised. Who are the people you would find it hardest to bring the gospel to, and what would it look like to go to them?
Simon wanted the power of God without a heart that was right before God. Where might you be drawn to the benefits of faith while resisting the surrender it asks?
God arranged for Philip to meet one seeking man on a desert road. How does it change your view of ordinary encounters to know God may have prepared them?
The eunuch went on his way rejoicing after hearing Christ from Isaiah and being baptized. What would it look like for your grasp of the gospel to lead you into that kind of joy?

translationNotes.note: The BSB does not include a verse 37 in the running text, moving from verse 36 to verse 38, because the earliest and best manuscripts lack it. A footnote records that the later Textus Receptus adds, And Philip said, If you believe with all your heart, you may be baptized. The eunuch replied, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. This study follows the BSB and carries the omission, noting the added words are a genuine and orthodox confession but not part of the earliest text.
Candace is not a personal name but a royal title, like Pharaoh, for the queen mother of the kingdom of the Nubians to the south of Egypt; the BSB footnote gives the Greek as Kandake.

The quotation follows the Greek of Isaiah 53:7-8. The phrase who can recount His descendants and For His life was removed from the earth reflect the Septuagint wording that Philip and Luke are citing.
